a_rows_sample.anchor:
each iteration introduces additional difficulty; knowledge operators do not automatically iterate. ... K(p)
ot\Rightarrow K(K(p)) ... K^n(p)
ot\Rightarrow K^{n+1}(p) ... Verified(x)\Rightarrow Verified(Verification(x)) [dangerous hidden assumption] ... Verification 
eq MetaVerification
a_rows_sample.statement: Epistemic Iteration Non-Closure: K^n(p) does not imply K^{n+1}(p) unless a separate rule/evidence/authority establishes the higher-order knowledge, guarding against 'the system knows X therefore it knows that it knows X'; applied to the Determination->Decision->Action->Observation->Verification chain to reject the hidden assumption Verified(x)=>Verified(Verification(x)), giving Verification != MetaVerification (Verify(V) requires its own evidence/context/authority). Status: [DERIVED].

a_rows_sample.anchor: EPISTEMIC LIMITS, ACCESSIBILITY AND KNOWLEDGE STANDING ... EL.1 Factivity [DECIDED/REINFORCED] ... EL.7 Structural Unknowability [PROP — strong research candidate] ... EL.8 Assertion Responsibility [PROP]
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes an 8-section theory addition 'EPISTEMIC LIMITS, ACCESSIBILITY AND KNOWLEDGE STANDING': EL.1 Factivity [DECIDED/REINFORCED], EL.2 Epistemic Non-Transparency [DERIVED], EL.3 Knowledge Iteration [DERIVED], EL.4 Evidence Relativity [PROP], EL.5 Margin of Error [PROP], EL.6 Accessibility (distinguishing Truth/Knowability/Accessibility/ActualKnowledge) [DERIVED], EL.7 Structural Unknowability [PROP-strong], EL.8 Assertion Responsibility [PROP], consolidating this file's individual candidates into one proposed section.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Mr Magoo sees a tree ... he cannot know for any i that the tree is not i inches tall ... Therefore, KK (knowledge that one knows) fails. ... Further iterations of knowledge are even harder to achieve.
a_rows_sample.statement: The Mr-Magoo margin-for-error argument formally derives the failure of the KK principle (knowledge does not imply knowledge of knowledge) via a step-by-step discrimination-limit argument, and notes iterations beyond the second are progressively harder to achieve -- the original formal source for the epistemic-iteration-non-closure principle.

a_rows_sample.anchor: What to Adopt: Knowledge First ✅ ... Evidence = Knowledge ✅ ... Factive Mental States ✅ ... Non-Luminosity ✅ ... Margin for Error ✅ ... Anti-KK ✅ ... Knowledge Rule for Assertion ✅ ... What to Reject: Knowledge = Justified True Belief ❌ ... Phenomenal Evidence ❌ ... Transparency of Rationality ❌ ... Luminosity of Mental States ❌ ... Recommendation: Integrate ... into KnowledgeOS Theory v1.2
a_rows_sample.statement: Final recommendation table adopts all seven listed concepts (Knowledge First, Evidence=Knowledge, Factive Mental States, Non-Luminosity, Margin for Error, Anti-KK, Knowledge Rule for Assertion) unconditionally (all checked, no [PROP]/[OPEN] hedging) and recommends integrating them directly into KnowledgeOS Theory v1.2 -- a materially stronger, less-hedged recommendation than the same-day review (S2528), which instead treats most of these as PROP-status research candidates and explicitly places 'Evidence=Knowledge' on its own rejection list.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Object level p ... Meta level Provable_S(p) ... Meta-meta level Provable_S(Provable_S(p)). These must not be automatically interchangeable. ... aligns beautifully with Williamson's finding K(p)\not\Rightarrow K(K(p)). ... Level Non-Collapse: L_n(x)\neq L_{n+1}(x) unless an explicit bridge is provided.
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes Object/Meta-level typing (p, Provable_S(p), Provable_S(Provable_S(p)) as distinct levels) and generalizes it into a core 'Level Non-Collapse' anti-collapse rule L_n(x) != L_{n+1}(x) absent an explicit bridge, explicitly noting this converges with (is a second independent reason for) Williamson's K(p) not=> K(K(p)); examples given: Truth(p)!=Provable_S(p), Provable_S(p)!=Known(Provable_S(p)), Verified(p)!=Verified(Verified(p)).

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'object-meta-level-non-collapse-principle' POSSIBLY relates to 'epistemic-iteration-non-closure' (batch B0061). Note: Candidate core anti-collapse principle: object-level p, meta-level Provable_S(p), and meta-meta-level Provable_S(Provable_S(p)) must not be automatically interchangeable absent an explicit bridge; explicitly aligned with Williamson's K(p) not=> K(K(p)) as a second independent reason for level separation, extended to Verified(p) != Verified(Verified(p)).

a_rows_sample.anchor: We will not yet build Zero, Lord or Sārathi. First we need to establish whether the epistemic foundation underneath them is computationally coherent. The experiment asks E \rightarrow Assessment \rightarrow Assertion and, crucially: When, if ever, may an Assertion enter Knowledge?
a_rows_sample.statement: Frames Step 25A.2's governing question: whether Evidence→Assessment→Assertion is computationally coherent and precisely when an Assertion may enter Knowledge, deliberately deferring Zero/Lord/Sārathi.

a_rows_sample.anchor:
First correction: Evidence is not itself a proposition ... The document is an artifact. The extracted statement is an observation. The proposition A_1: Version(Nexus)=3.69.0 is an assertion. Artifact 
eq Observation 
eq Evidence 
eq Assertion. They may refer to the same underlying information, bu
a_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms Artifact≠Observation≠Evidence≠Assertion as four domain-meaning-distinct concepts even when referring to the same underlying information.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Minimal Evidence type ... E=(id, source, content, observedAt, acquiredAt, method, provenance). Status: PROPOSED. We will test whether this is sufficient. ... Assertion type ... A=(id, proposition, context, temporalScope). Version(Nexus)=3.69 without context is potentially ambiguous.
a_rows_sample.statement: Refines the minimal Evidence type to E=(id,source,content,observedAt,acquiredAt,method,provenance) and Assertion to A=(id,proposition,context,temporalScope), noting an assertion without context can be ambiguous.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Assessment ... Q(E,A,C) where Q assesses how the evidence relates to the assertion. We deliberately do not initially define Q as a single probability. Instead, we separate dimensions. Q=(Relevance,Reliability,Directness,TemporalValidity,Consistency,Authenticity). Status: EXPERIMENTAL. ... Why multid
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the six-dimension Assessment Q=(Relevance,Reliability,Directness,TemporalValidity,Consistency,Authenticity), deliberately not a single probability, illustrated by an authentic-but-stale document where a scalar confidence would hide the temporal-validity/authenticity split.

a_rows_sample.anchor: First evidence experiment ... K_0=\varnothing. E_1: Version(Nexus)=3.69.0. Assessment: Relevance high, Directness direct, Authenticity established, Temporal current, Conflict none. Then produce A_1. At this stage A_1 is supported, but we should be careful with the word "true". ... Supported versus t
a_rows_sample.statement: Works the first single-evidence experiment producing A1 with status Supported (not Truth), reaffirming Supported is an epistemic state distinct from metaphysical truth to preserve epistemic humility.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Second experiment — corroboration ... E_2: Version(Nexus)=3.69.0 from an independent source. We have corroboration. But here we encounter our first major statistical issue. ... Independence cannot be assumed ... Suppose E_1 is a document copied from E_2 ... E_1=f(E_2). EvidenceCount=2 does not imply
a_rows_sample.statement: Works a corroboration experiment then immediately undermines naive counting: EvidenceCount=2 does not imply IndependentEvidenceCount=2 if one item was copied from the other.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Evidence dependency ... DependsOn(E_i,E_j) or more generally EvidenceGraph. Then corroboration can distinguish Independent E_1\perp E_2 from Derived/copy E_2=f(E_1). Status: REQUIRED CONCEPT but its exact mathematical representation remains unresolved.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a DependsOn(Ei,Ej) relation / EvidenceGraph as a REQUIRED CONCEPT distinguishing independent from derived/copied evidence, with its exact mathematical representation left unresolved.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Third experiment — contradiction ... E_3: Version(Nexus)=3.72.0 ... A_1: Version=3.69 and A_2: Version=3.72. They cannot both hold under the same context/time semantics. Conflict(A_1,A_2) must be generated. ... What must NOT happen ... Latest source wins. Highest confidence wins. Majority vote wins.
a_rows_sample.statement: Works a direct contradiction experiment requiring an explicit Conflict object, explicitly rejecting five naive resolution strategies (latest-wins, highest-confidence-wins, majority-vote, LLM-decides, averaging) as none universally valid.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Correct intermediate state ... Assertion A1 Version = 3.69 Supported by E1,E2 ... Assertion A2 Version = 3.72 Supported by E3 ... Conflict A1 ↔ A2. Then the system asks: Is the conflict resolvable under the available rules/context/time?
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows the correct intermediate representation retaining both conflicting assertions with their evidence and an explicit Conflict marker, asking whether the conflict is resolvable under rules/context/time.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Conflict resolution ... E_3 is a direct current system query at t_3 while E_1 is an old inventory at t_1<t_3. Now the contradiction may disappear if the assertions have different validity intervals. A_1: Valid:[t_1,t_2] and A_2: Valid:[t_3,\infty). Then NoLogicalConflict exists. It was a temporal ap
a_rows_sample.statement: Resolves the apparent contradiction by discovering the two assertions have disjoint validity intervals — 'temporal apparent conflict' — proving conflict must be defined as f(A1,A2,Context,Time,Scope), never merely A1≠A2, a major result to formalize.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Fourth experiment — stale evidence ... E_4: Version=3.69 was obtained six months ago. For What version was running six months ago? it may be excellent evidence. For What version is running now? it may be insufficient. Therefore Assessment(E,A,P,t) must depend on the purpose/question. ... Assessment
a_rows_sample.statement: Works a stale-evidence experiment showing the same evidence can be excellent for a historical question and insufficient for a current one, refining Assessment to Q(E,A,P,C,t) with purpose P and evaluation time t added.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Fifth experiment — LLM output ... L_1: "Nexus backup is verified." No supporting artifact exists. We create A_3: BackupVerified=True. But its support relation is Support(A_3)=\{LLMOutput\}. Therefore Assessment(A_3)=Unsupported. It remains a candidate assertion. It does not enter committed knowledge
a_rows_sample.statement: Works an unsupported-LLM-claim experiment: support relation is only {LLMOutput}, so Assessment(A3)=Unsupported and it never enters committed knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Sixth experiment — LLM correctly extracts evidence ... Backup verification report: Backup completed successfully at 03:00. The LLM extracts A_4: BackupCompleted=True. This is different. The LLM is now an interpretation mechanism. The actual supporting evidence is the source document. Therefore prove
a_rows_sample.statement: Contrasts the previous hallucination case with a legitimate LLM-extraction-from-a-real-document case: provenance must be A4→LLMExtraction→Document, not merely A4→LLM, distinguishing transformation from source.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Seventh experiment — summary ... Summary(Document)=S. The summary says: "Backup is operational." But the original document contains important qualifications. KnowledgeOS must not treat S as equivalent to Document. Therefore Summary\rightarrow SourceArtifact must remain traceable.
a_rows_sample.statement: Works a summary-vs-source experiment requiring Summary≠Document with traceability Summary→SourceArtifact preserved (reaffirming the earlier DerivedSummary≠SourceEvidence invariant).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Eighth experiment — authenticity ... an artifact has a valid digital signature. Then Authenticity=True. Does that imply Assertion=True? No. It establishes something about the artifact's origin/integrity, not necessarily the truth of its content. Authenticity\neq Truth.
a_rows_sample.statement: Works a digital-signature experiment reaffirming Authenticity ≠ Truth — a valid signature proves origin/integrity, not content truth.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Ninth experiment — authority ... a document is authentic and contains: "Migration is approved." But the author has no authority to approve migration. Then Authenticity=True but Authority=False. Authenticity\neq Authority. This connects Evidence directly to our later governance model.
a_rows_sample.statement: Works an authority-vs-authenticity experiment (an authentic document from an unauthorized author) reaffirming Authenticity≠Authority, connecting to the governance model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Tenth experiment — statistical evidence ... 98, 101, 99. \bar{x}=99.33. But now suppose 140 comes from a fourth instrument known to have calibration problems. The correct epistemic representation cannot simply be Mean=109.5. We need measurement provenance; measurement reliability; uncertainty; poten
a_rows_sample.statement: Works a statistical outlier experiment (three consistent measurements plus one from a known-faulty instrument) confirming naive averaging (Mean=109.5) is wrong — evidence aggregation cannot be simple counting, requiring provenance/reliability/uncertainty/measurement model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Eleventh experiment — evidence dependence ... Website ↓ PDF ↓ LLM summary ↓ Human report. All four claim A. A naive system sees 4 sources. The actual system has approximately 1 underlying information lineage. NumberOfSources\neq AmountOfIndependentEvidence. This is a major statistical requirement.
a_rows_sample.statement: Works a four-link-derivation-chain experiment (website→PDF→LLM summary→human report all claiming the same thing) showing four apparent sources collapse to roughly one underlying lineage — NumberOfSources≠AmountOfIndependentEvidence.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Twelfth experiment — negative evidence ... E_1: BackupVerified=True. Another test returns E_2: BackupRestoreTest=Failed. The second item does not necessarily mean BackupExists=False. It may mean BackupExists=True but Restorability=False. Therefore evidence interpretation requires precise proposition
a_rows_sample.statement: Works a negative-evidence experiment showing a failed restore test does not falsify backup-existence but rather a distinct proposition (restorability), requiring precisely typed/semantically-distinct assertions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: This reveals a deeper principle ... Evidence does not directly modify truth. It modifies the epistemic state associated with propositions. E \rightarrow Assessment(A) \rightarrow K not E\rightarrow Reality. Reality changes through actions/events, not through our assessment.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the deeper principle that evidence modifies epistemic state, not reality itself (E→Assessment(A)→K, never E→Reality) — reality changes only through actions/events.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 25A is not yet a test of the whole KnowledgeOS theory. It is the first controlled experiment to see whether the minimal formal state and type system can represent the epistemic cycle without semantic contradictions. I attempted to execute the first prototype in the current environment, but the
b_rows_sample.statement: Discloses that a first prototype execution attempt did NOT successfully complete in the available environment, explicitly refusing to claim experimental results not actually obtained — proceeding instead with conceptual/formal work only, to be executed in a later tool-capable environment.

b_rows_sample.anchor: What is the smallest state required to represent KnowledgeOS without losing the distinctions established in the theory? I propose that we start with nine fundamental types, rather than implementing the much larger list.
b_rows_sample.statement: Poses the minimality question and commits to nine fundamental types rather than the much larger 21-type list proposed in the prior handover file.

b_rows_sample.anchor: WorldState W_t Represents the state of the external subject/world at time t. W_t(Nexus.version)=3.69.0. Important: W_t \neq K_t because KnowledgeOS may not know the true world state.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines WorldState W_t (worked with Nexus.version example), reaffirming W_t≠K_t.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Observation O An observation is something obtained from interacting with or observing the world. Minimal form: O=(id,subject,value,time,method,source). Observation subject = nexus.version, value = 3.69.0, time = 10:00, method = infrastructure_inventory. An observation is not yet knowledge.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Observation O=(id,subject,value,time,method,source), explicitly not yet knowledge.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Evidence E Evidence is information that is being used to support or challenge a proposition. Minimal form: E=(id,proposition,content,origin,time,provenance). E_1: Nexus.version=3.69.0 from an infrastructure inventory. Critically: Observation\neq Evidence. An observation may become evidence, but the
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Evidence E=(id,proposition,content,origin,time,provenance), reaffirming Observation≠Evidence with the distinction required to remain visible even when an observation becomes evidence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Assertion A An assertion is a proposition that can be evaluated. A_1: Nexus.version=3.69.0. It has a relationship to evidence: E\rightarrow A. But A\neq Knowledge. An assertion may be candidate, supported, conflicted, committed, retracted. This is already enough to expose an important question: What
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Assertion A with a five-value status set (candidate/supported/conflicted/committed/retracted), reaffirming A≠Knowledge and explicitly leaving open what makes an assertion eligible for commitment.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Assessment Q Assessment records the epistemic evaluation of an assertion. Q(A,E,C) \rightarrow Assessment. It may eventually contain support, confidence, reliability, uncertainty, method. But we should not yet invent a probability algebra. That belongs to the later statistical work.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Assessment as Q(A,E,C)→Assessment with five candidate future fields, deliberately deferring any probability algebra to later statistical work.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeState K_t At minimum K_t = (A_t,Q_t,E_t,C_t,P_t) where assertions; assessments; relevant evidence; conflicts; provenance/lineage. This is deliberately provisional. [UNRESOLVED] Is evidence actually part of K_t, or is it external to the knowledge state and merely referenced by it? We should
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the provisional KnowledgeState K_t=(Assertions,Assessments,Evidence,Conflicts,Provenance), explicitly flagging [UNRESOLVED] whether Evidence belongs inside K_t or is merely referenced, to be settled by testing against historical reconstruction/retraction/provenance/conflict-resolution requirements, not by intuition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Goal G A goal specifies what we want to achieve. G="Prepare Nexus for governed migration." A goal is not an action. Goal\neq Action.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Goal G, reaffirming Goal≠Action.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge Requirement R A requirement specifies what must be established for the purpose. R_1=BackupVerified, R_2=RollbackVerified, R_3=ArchitectureApproval. Then R(G)=\{R_1,R_2,R_3\}.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines KnowledgeRequirement R worked with a three-item migration requirement set R(G).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Epistemic Contract C_G The contract defines what "enough knowledge" means for this goal. C_G=\{R(G),Criticality,TemporalRequirements,AuthorityRequirements\}. Then Sufficient(K_t,C_G) becomes computable in principle. This is much stronger than asking "Does KnowledgeOS know enough?" because enough for
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines EpistemicContract C_G=(R(G),Criticality,TemporalRequirements,AuthorityRequirements), making Sufficient(K_t,C_G) computable in principle, stronger than an unqualified 'know enough?' question.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Minimal State So our first experimental state becomes: K_t=(E_t,A_t,Q_t,C_t,P_t,V_t) with G and C_G outside the knowledge state as the purpose/decision context. But I want to flag this as PROVISIONAL rather than established.
b_rows_sample.statement: Refines the minimal state to K_t=(E_t,A_t,Q_t,C_t,P_t,V_t) with Goal and EpistemicContract kept external as purpose/decision context, explicitly flagged PROVISIONAL, not established.

b_rows_sample.anchor: First state transition ... Observe(W_t) \rightarrow O then O \rightarrow E then E \rightarrow Assessment then Assessment \rightarrow Assertion then potentially Assertion \rightarrow K_{t+1}. Therefore K_{t+1} = Update(K_t,E,A,Q,C) is our first executable transition.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the first executable transition chain Observe→O→E→Assessment→Assertion→K_{t+1}, formalized as K_{t+1}=Update(K_t,E,A,Q,C).

b_rows_sample.anchor: First experiment ... K_0=\varnothing. Observation Nexus version = 3.69.0. Evidence E_1: Version(Nexus)=3.69.0. Assessment Evidence supports the assertion. Assertion A_1: Version(Nexus)=3.69.0. Commit K_1 contains the committed assertion. K_0 \xrightarrow{E_1} K_1.
b_rows_sample.statement: Walks through the smallest possible experiment from empty K_0 through a single evidence item to committed K_1.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Now we attack it ... E_2: Version(Nexus)=3.72.0. Now we have E_1\Rightarrow A_1 and E_2\Rightarrow A_2 where A_1\neq A_2. The system must produce Conflict(Version(Nexus)) rather than silently replacing 3.69.0 with 3.72.0. This is our first adversarial test.
b_rows_sample.statement: Designs the first adversarial test (a second contradicting version value) expecting an explicit Conflict marker rather than silent replacement.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Second attack — LLM ... Nexus has a verified backup. but there is no evidence supporting BackupVerified=True. Therefore LLMOutput \rightarrow CandidateAssertion but not LLMOutput \rightarrow CommittedKnowledge. Expected: Status=Unsupported or equivalent. This tests one of our strongest invariants.
b_rows_sample.statement: Designs the second adversarial test (unsupported LLM claim) expecting Status=Unsupported, testing the LLM-output/committed-knowledge boundary.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Third attack — temporal reasoning ... At t_0 we know Version=3.69. At t_1 we learn Version=3.72. The correct result is not "The old evidence was wrong." It may have been historically correct. Therefore the model needs ValidAt(E,t). This is the first indication that temporal validity is not optional.
b_rows_sample.statement: Designs the third adversarial test (successive true version changes over time), requiring ValidAt(E,t) rather than treating the older value as simply wrong — the first concrete indication that temporal validity is not optional.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Fourth attack — retraction ... E_1 is later invalidated. Retract(E_1). We cannot simply delete E_1. We must find Dependents(E_1). Then recompute affected assertions. This gives us Retraction \rightarrow DependencyAnalysis \rightarrow KnowledgeRevision.
b_rows_sample.statement: Designs the fourth adversarial test (retraction), requiring Dependents(E1) computation and recomputation of affected assertions rather than deletion.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Fifth attack — sufficiency ... K_t contains Version, Backup but not Rollback and ArchitectureApproval. Then Sufficient(K_t,C_G)=False. The important point is that we don't need universal knowledge. We only need to evaluate the explicit contract.
b_rows_sample.statement: Designs the fifth adversarial test (partial requirement satisfaction), showing Sufficient(K_t,C_G)=False evaluates only against the explicit contract, not universal knowledge.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Sixth attack — more knowledge ... The test returns Rollback=False. Previously Rollback=Unknown. Knowledge increased. But readiness remains false, and possibly becomes more decisively false. Thus the simulation should demonstrate |K_{t+1}|>|K_t| while Readiness(K_{t+1}) < Readiness(K_t) is possible.
b_rows_sample.statement: Designs the sixth adversarial test (rollback test failing), formalizing the key property |K_{t+1}|>|K_t| while Readiness(K_{t+1})<Readiness(K_t) can simultaneously hold.

b_aliases: Step 25A.1: Minimal Formal State and Type System

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'evidence-assessment-assertion-pipeline' POSSIBLY relates to 'minimal-formal-state-type-system' (batch B0021). Note: S0887's Step 25A.2: twelve worked thought-experiments testing the Evidence->Assessment->Assertion pipeline, refining Assessment to a purpose/time-relativized, finite-valued, nine-field non-scalar object; a temporal-apparent-conflict resolution; five rejected naive conflict-resolution strategies; LLM-as-interpretation-mechanism provenance; the epistemic_status=committed (never truth=true) naming principle; a conservative Commit(A) rule tested on five cases; verdicts PASS WITH REFINEMENTS REQUIRED with U1-U8 open items; refines the theory's chain to Evidence->Assessment->Assertion->Commitment->KnowledgeState; hands off to Step 25A.3 (revision/conflict/temporal validity/retraction).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Expressiveness <-> Tractability ... reasoning by cases can become computationally explosive
a_rows_sample.statement: Candidate Theory-level methodological principle: a KnowledgeOS representation is not justified merely because it is semantically expressive; its reasoning consequences and computational tractability must be explicitly considered — an independent formal reason to resist building one universal semantic structure.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Expressiveness does not justify computational complexity by itself ... Semantic question: What distinctions can the representation express? Computational question: What reasoning can be performed over it, with what guarantees and cost? Neither question substitutes for the other.
a_rows_sample.statement: Methodological principle: expressiveness does not justify computational complexity by itself; every proposed KnowledgeOS semantic mechanism must separately answer a semantic question (what distinctions can it express) and a computational question (what reasoning can be performed, with what guarantees/cost) — neither substitutes for the other, grounded in KR&R's expressiveness/tractability tradeoff and reasoning-by-cases explosion.

a_rows_sample.anchor: There is a tradeoff between the expressiveness of a representation language and the difficulty of reasoning ... A slight increase in the expressiveness of a Description Logic may result in a drastic change in the complexity of reasoning.
a_rows_sample.statement: Expressiveness/tractability tradeoff restated with a concrete 'computational cliff' example: adding role restriction to FL- makes subsumption coNP-hard, versus polynomial without it — offered as underlying principle for [PROP]-status constructs in KnowledgeOS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Semantic expressiveness and computational tractability must be evaluated separately ... A richer representation is not automatically a better KnowledgeOS representation ... a candidate kernel operation is not admissible merely because it is semantically elegant. It must satisfy: Expressiveness+Soundness+Completeness_declared-domain+ComplexityBound
a_rows_sample.statement: Derives a kernel-selection criterion from the expressiveness/tractability tradeoff: a candidate kernel operation must satisfy Expressiveness + Soundness + Completeness_(declared domain) + ComplexityBound where appropriate; explicit warning that tableau soundness/completeness for a specified DL semantics does not imply KnowledgeOS as a whole can or should be complete. Kernel remains NOT SELECTABLE; this is a selection criterion, not a kernel definition.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KR.1 Representation Layers ... KR.6 Open-World Constraint ... KR.9 Transition ... KR.10 Expressiveness and Tractability
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes inserting a 10-section 'KNOWLEDGE REPRESENTATION AND STRUCTURED REASONING' theory addition (KR.1 Representation Layers, KR.2 Reasoning Cn_S, KR.3 Subsumption, KR.4 Classification, KR.5 Consistency, KR.6 Open-World Constraint, KR.7 Evaluation via reasoning-service family, KR.8 Explanation/Missing Assumptions, KR.9 Transition/successor-state with Boundary!=FrameAxiom retained, KR.10 Expressiveness/Tractability), consolidating all the file's individually-derived candidates into one proposed section.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KR.1 Representation Layers [PROP] ... KR.6 Open-World Constraint [ESTABLISHED] — Supported by DL's open-world semantics ... KR.10 Expressiveness and Tractability [ESTABLISHED] — Now a KnowledgeOS methodological principle
a_rows_sample.statement: Restates the ten-section KR.1-KR.10 theory insertion verbatim from S2523 with an explicit status tag assigned to each section: KR.1 Representation [PROP], KR.2 Reasoning [PROP], KR.3 Subsumption [PROP], KR.4 Classification [PROP], KR.5 Consistency [PROP], KR.6 Open-World Constraint promoted to [ESTABLISHED], KR.7 Evaluation [PROP], KR.8 Explanation/Gap [PROP], KR.9 Transition [PROP] (Boundary != FrameAxiom retained), KR.10 Expressiveness/Tractability promoted to [ESTABLISHED] as a KnowledgeOS methodological principle -- the only two sections elevated above [PROP].

b_rows_sample.anchor: "Zero can be understood as a form of CWA." ... I would explicitly reject that translation for now.
b_rows_sample.statement: Rejects the extraction's claim 'Zero = CWA' given prior Zero experiments established Unknown != Absent, NoEvidence != EvidenceOfAbsence, Unresolved != False; instead proposes CWA as a useful comparator via the test Zero_KO =? CWA, expected to strengthen Zero by documenting why they differ. Default reasoning (CWA, circumscription, default logic, autoepistemic logic) should NOT be added as a KnowledgeOS primitive yet — there is no single universal way of reasoning from incomplete information.

b_rows_sample.statement: KnowledgeOS adopts Unknown != False as a methodological constraint, since K⊭p does not generally imply K⊨¬p and CWA is one particular convention among several approaches to default reasoning (not a consequence of incomplete knowledge itself); consequently Zero != CWA unless a future adjudicated theory explicitly establishes such an identification — important because Zero is retained as a candidate epistemic-boundary construct, not a settled primitive.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The fact that absence of information in an ABox only indicates lack of knowledge... is why queries are more complex than database queries. ... This is why Zero ≠ CWA. ... A concept description can also be conceived as a query ... requirements are just concept descriptions.
b_rows_sample.statement: Cites the handbook's open-world reasoning point (absence of information in an ABox indicates lack of knowledge, not negation, unlike closed database queries) as direct support for Zero != CWA; also cites 'subsumption is the fundamental reasoning task, organizing knowledge into a taxonomy' and 'a concept description can be conceived as a query' to argue requirements are concept descriptions and queries.

b_rows_sample.statement: Open-world DL result (absence of information indicates lack of knowledge, not negation) independently supports Unknown != False and NoEvidence != EvidenceOfAbsence, aligned with prior Zero experiments; proposes splitting Zero analysis into logical absence (K⊭p) versus explicit negation (K⊨¬p) as distinct levels, reinforcing Unknown != Absent, Unresolved != False — Zero remains OPEN but theoretically strengthened.

b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes inserting a 10-section 'KNOWLEDGE REPRESENTATION AND STRUCTURED REASONING' theory addition (KR.1 Representation Layers, KR.2 Reasoning Cn_S, KR.3 Subsumption, KR.4 Classification, KR.5 Consistency, KR.6 Open-World Constraint, KR.7 Evaluation via reasoning-service family, KR.8 Explanation/Missing Assumptions, KR.9 Transition/successor-state with Boundary!=FrameAxiom retained, KR.10 Expressiveness/Tractability), consolidating all the file's individually-derived candidates into one proposed section.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Complete satisfaction = executable situation ... Executability means Poss(e,K) or that all actions in a history were possible. Zero is our much broader boundary/incompleteness concept. ... Zero\neq Executability ... Executable \rightarrow one possible input to a Zero analysis
b_rows_sample.statement: Rejects 'Zero = executable situation' as 'the most important incorrect mapping in the document': executability (Poss(e,K) holding for all actions in a history) does not entail completeness of a boundary/incompleteness analysis; restates prior Zero invariants (Unknown!=Absent, NoEvidence!=EvidenceOfAbsence, Conflict!=Invalidity, UnknownDimension!=UnknownValue) and concludes Zero != Executability, with Executable at most one possible input to a Zero analysis.

b_rows_sample.anchor: anti-luminosity: roughly, the assumption that whenever a condition obtains, one is automatically in a position to know that it obtains. His argument uses reliability, limited discrimination and sorites-style reasoning. ... EvidenceExists(e) not=> EvaluatorCanEstablish(EvidenceExists(e)) ... Zero(K)=0 not=> Known(Zero(K)=0). This is very important for Zero.
b_rows_sample.statement: Applies the non-transparency principle specifically to Zero and consistency/completeness: EvidenceExists(e) not=> EvaluatorCanEstablish(EvidenceExists(e)); Consistent(K) not=> Known(Consistent(K)); Complete(K) not=> Known(Complete(K)); Zero(K)=0 not=> Known(Zero(K)=0) -- i.e. even if a knowledge base actually has zero gap, the system may be unable to know that it has zero gap.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A knowledge base represents what is explicitly believed; what is implicitly believed is what follows from it. ... Tell(KB,\alpha)\rightarrow KB' ... Ask(KB,\alpha)\rightarrow \{Yes,No,Unknown\} ... Only-Knowing — A formal logic for "all I know" — exactly what you need for Zero
b_rows_sample.statement: Recommends Levesque & Lakemeyer's Logic of Knowledge Bases as second priority, proposing its TELL/ASK interface (with the unhedged three-valued ASK return type later replaced by Eval_c in S2520/S2521) and its 'Only-Knowing' formal logic for 'all I know' as directly relevant to the open Zero TODO and the Closed-World-Assumption question.

b_rows_sample.anchor:
a person may retain a justified determination while no longer possessing or remembering the original evidence ... UnavailableEvidence 
eq AbsentEvidence ... NotAccessible(e)
eq NotExisting(e) ... NoEvidence 
eq EvidenceUnavailable 
eq EvidenceForgotten 
eq EvidenceOfAbsence
b_rows_sample.statement: Extends the Zero invariant family with UnavailableEvidence != AbsentEvidence and NotAccessible(e) != NotExisting(e), giving a four-way split NoEvidence != EvidenceUnavailable != EvidenceForgotten != EvidenceOfAbsence, reinforcing similar findings already independently reached from Williamson and Godel in this batch.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Surprising evidence should not simply be dismissed because it conflicts with the existing knowledge structure ... Conflict \not\Rightarrow RejectNewEvidence ... Conflict\rightarrow Reassessment\rightarrow Revision rather than Conflict\rightarrow False ... contradiction is a trigger for epistemic examination, not automatically a verdict of invalidity.
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues against treating coherence as the sole epistemic criterion: surprising/conflicting evidence should trigger Conflict->Reassessment->Revision rather than an automatic Conflict->False verdict, directly relevant to Contr/Zero/lifecycle/revision and consistent with the project's own prior FDE research.

b_rows_sample.anchor: What This Book Confirms: Sat | Entailment: K_t \models Content(r) ... Zero | Complete knowledge under closed-world assumption ... Contr | Knowledge of contradictions; inconsistency detection ... Lifecycle | Nonmonotonicity
b_rows_sample.statement: Unhedged 'what this book confirms' table asserting Sat=Entailment (K_t |= Content(r)) and Zero='complete knowledge under closed-world assumption' -- the same overclaim pattern (Sat=Entailment, Zero=CWA) already explicitly rejected in the DL-handbook and Williamson threads elsewhere in this batch (S2520, S2528, S2530), here recurring in the raw Reiter extraction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KOS-NEXT-ACTOR-ORCHESTRATION-001 / AST-018 (SEPARATE, EXISTING, UNCHANGED) ... KOS-OPERATING-MODEL-001 (NEW — this recording) ... The new slice CONSUMES AST-018 as the existing canonical mechanism for next-actor orchestration. It does not modify, re-implement, re-open, or await the adoption of AST-018.
a_rows_sample.statement: PO/ARB's Option-B decision explicitly creates a separate governed slice (the operating model) that consumes, rather than modifies or waits on, the existing AST-018 slice; AST-018's own STOP→verification→adoption path continues unaffected in parallel.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Responsibilities, not services/positions ... Neither name enters the declared workflow role vocabulary consumed by AST-015/AST-017/AST-018 ... without an explicit governed decision
a_rows_sample.statement: Five recorded review constraints bind the coming implementation: Governance Engineer/Communication Engineer must remain operating responsibilities (never platform services or organizational positions, per the adopted six-role non-equivalence); neither name may silently enter the workflow role vocabulary; REVIEW_INDEPENDENCE_POLICY stays a placeholder; layer scope needs explicit PO/ARB confirmation; and the AST-018 slice's own obligations are not displaced by the new work item.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The Governance Engineer is the dedicated human-facing governance role ... The Communication Engineer is NOT a permanent person. It is a TRANSFERABLE OPERATIONAL RESPONSIBILITY. Any currently authorized actor/session may perform the Communication Engineer responsibility for routine coordination.
a_rows_sample.statement: The operating model defines two human-facing responsibilities: a dedicated Governance Engineer (business/authority/exception handling, adoption presentation) and a transferable Communication Engineer (routine session-lifecycle coordination performable by any currently authorized actor), with the rule BUSINESS/AUTHORITY/EXCEPTION→Governance, ROUTINE/OPERATIONAL/SESSION-COORDINATION→Communication, HUMAN AUTHORITY→Human/PO-ARB.

a_rows_sample.anchor: This produces exactly one business-level outcome: CONTINUE, PERMISSION_REQUIRED, FRESH_SESSION_REQUIRED, GOVERNANCE_DECISION_REQUIRED, STOP. ... Do NOT create a second workflow-state vocabulary.
a_rows_sample.statement: Every working session's local governance/communication capability at completion must classify its situation into exactly one of five business-level outcomes (CONTINUE / PERMISSION_REQUIRED / FRESH_SESSION_REQUIRED / GOVERNANCE_DECISION_REQUIRED / STOP), explicitly forbidden from becoming a second, competing workflow-state vocabulary.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A process identity is: DISCOVERED FROM THE RUNTIME. It is not: invented by the human; copied from another session; inferred from prompt text; chosen from a human-entered UUID. ... Therefore: role ≠ process identity; identity ≠ eligibility; eligibility ≠ appointment; appointment ≠ activation; activation ≠ authorization.
a_rows_sample.statement: The Process Identity Rule: the human always chooses business intent/role, and the runtime always supplies concrete process identity — never the reverse — yielding a five-term non-equivalence chain (role≠identity≠eligibility≠appointment≠activation≠authorization) that must never collapse.

a_rows_sample.anchor: MATCH ... 'This is the assigned session. You may continue.' ... MISMATCH ... 'This is not the session assigned to this work.' Then: 1. Open the assigned session 2. Prepare the exact prompt for the assigned session 3. Stop.
a_rows_sample.statement: When an actor is already appointed, a fresh session's runtime identity is compared against the expected actor to produce exactly ACTOR_MATCH or ACTOR_MISMATCH; on mismatch the system must never create a second appointment, replace or impersonate the appointed actor, self-register, or treat the mismatch itself as authorization — it only offers a business-language recovery path.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Do not hard-code in this implementation whether every review must be: same session, subagent, independent OS session. Treat review independence as a separate policy. The implementation must support the concept: REVIEW_INDEPENDENCE_POLICY but must not invent final policy rules.
a_rows_sample.statement: The degree of review independence required (same session / subagent / independent OS session) is deliberately left as an unresolved, named policy placeholder (REVIEW_INDEPENDENCE_POLICY) rather than hard-coded, so the implementation supports the concept without inventing the final rule.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Do not treat verification as adoption. Do not treat review PASS as adoption.
a_rows_sample.statement: Final adoption requires an explicit human decision (Accept/Adopt, Return, or Stop) presented by the Governance Engineer after review PASS; review passing and independent verification are each explicitly insufficient on their own to constitute adoption.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The human must never need to: provide a session UUID; choose runtime process identity; determine mutationOwner; determine predecessor; construct REGISTER; construct HANDOFF; construct START; edit workflow JSON; invoke workflow-state.php; inspect workflow records to route the work; diagnose INV-B; diagnose G-3; understand token/tokenRef; manually calculate authorization.
a_rows_sample.statement: A fourteen-item hard acceptance criterion enumerates everything the human must never be required to do; if the human is forced to perform any of these in a normal workflow, the implementation is declared to have failed the human-facing contract.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Explicitly distinguish: IMPLEMENTED from: ADOPTED and: AUTHORIZED for future use. Do not collapse them.
a_rows_sample.statement: Every completion report produced under this operating model must keep IMPLEMENTED, VERIFIED, ADOPTED and AUTHORIZED as four distinct, never-collapsed states — a rule enforced verbatim through every subsequent artifact in the batch (implementation, AMENDMENT-001, and their completion reports).

a_rows_sample.anchor: the capability layer is minimal. The operating model is the primary deliverable; it consumes the existing AST-018 commands and does not re-implement, enlarge, or re-open them. Any new software produced under this commission is minimal support for the operating model — never a second workflow engine
a_rows_sample.statement: PO/ARB authorizes all three delivery layers (operating model document, minimal supporting capability, verification/acceptance) but clarifies 'minimal supporting capability' to mean the new software must consume AST-018's existing commands rather than re-implement or enlarge them.

a_rows_sample.anchor: test_om_37 proves all four canonical assets byte-unchanged vs HEAD. PO/ARB's two corrected semantics pinned in tests: FRESH_SESSION_REQUIRED = paste-prompt-not-appointment (+ no UUID asked); session candidate status never inferred from UNRESOLVED + NEXT_ACTOR_REQUIRED.
a_rows_sample.statement: The completed implementation records two specific PO/ARB-corrected semantic pins in its test suite: FRESH_SESSION_REQUIRED means presenting a paste-ready prompt, not an appointment act, and never asking for a UUID; and a session's candidate status must never be silently inferred merely from an UNRESOLVED bootstrap plus a NEXT_ACTOR_REQUIRED result.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The work item is STOPPED (seq 4) — an explicit CONTINUATION (recordedBy governance/human) must precede any REGISTER(verification); this prompt creates no activation.
a_rows_sample.statement: The candidate-declaration prompt for a fresh verifier explicitly states that STOPPED is sticky and that an explicit, human-recorded CONTINUATION must occur before any REGISTER(verification) can be written, listing nine barred prior participants including the implementing session itself.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The producer's completion report §38 was itself a verification object — its four-state separation (IMPLEMENTED ≠ VERIFIED ≠ ADOPTED ≠ AUTHORIZED) had to be accurate in content, not just in label.
a_rows_sample.statement: Independent verification treats a completion report's own claimed status-separation as itself a falsifiable object, not merely a label to trust — confirming the producer's IMPLEMENTED/NOT-VERIFIED/NOT-ADOPTED/NOT-AUTHORIZED claims held true in substance, not only in wording.

a_rows_sample.anchor: If the verifier also performed the adoption review, VERIFIED and ADOPTED-review would collapse into one actor — the exact collapse the operating model forbids.
a_rows_sample.statement: The verifier itself refuses to perform the Governance adoption review, extending the producer-bar/separation-of-duties chain a further step: a verifier acting as its own adoption reviewer would collapse two of the operating model's four distinct states (VERIFIED, ADOPTED) into a single actor's judgement, which §38 explicitly forbids.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Human{Developer,Domain Architect,Architecture Board,Governance,Operations} → KnowledgeOS{AI Agents,Assurance,Governance,Engineering Systems}. Who does what, who owns the resulting knowledge, who can decide, and what evidence must exist before the next step is allowed?
b_rows_sample.statement: Opens Step 156 (KnowledgeOS Operating Model): shifts from a primarily technical artifact to defining how humans, AI agents, governance bodies, and engineering systems interact day-to-day, connecting directly to the Domain Architect/Architecture Board/Softwareeinführungsprozess/IT Change Management governance work developed elsewhere.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge → Context → Inquiry → Decision → Action → Observation → Evidence → Assurance → Learning, under Governance. Governance → Knowledge → Engineering → Evidence → Governance.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the fundamental operating equation and the primary organizational feedback loop, reframing Step 156 from 'who uses KnowledgeOS' to how governed knowledge moves through the organization while preserving authority, provenance, accountability.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Human{Developer,Domain Architect,Architecture Board/Governance,Operations}, AI{Engineering/Architecture/Analysis/Assurance-support agents}, System{repositories,CI/CD,runtime,monitoring,infrastructure,external systems}. Actor ≠ Authority. AI Agent ≠ Governance Authority.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines five operating actor categories across Human/AI/System, rejecting a simple 'users vs system' model.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Know (what is believed/declared true?), Decide (what should be permitted/required?), Act (what should be changed?), Assure (did reality conform?). Know→Decide→Act→Assure, with evidence flowing back into knowledge.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines four responsibility classes and the KnowledgeOS responsibility triangle (Authority decides at the apex, Knowledge<->Action on one axis, Assurance verifying below).

b_rows_sample.anchor: AI may reason, humans remain accountable (unless explicitly delegated) — an authority-boundary principle, not an anti-AI principle.
b_rows_sample.statement: States human accountability for authority-requiring decisions; defines the AI operating role as Observe/Understand/Retrieve/Reason/Propose/Execute-where-authorized/Report, explicitly not Invent authority/Change governance/Rewrite authoritative knowledge/Hide uncertainty/Declare itself correct, formalized as AI Capability ⊆ AuthorizedActionSpace.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Agent = Role + Context + Authority + Constraints + Capabilities + EvidenceRequirements. AgentContext{Identity,Role,Task,Knowledge,Provenance,Applicable Rules,Authority,Constraints,Available Tools,Allowed Actions,Evidence Requirements,Verification Requirements}. An agent should never receive only prompt+tools.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the agent operating contract as an important refinement of agent architecture; worked example — 'upgrade Nexus' is not yet a valid action until KnowledgeOS resolves which Nexus/environment/version/approved target/applicable architecture/change process/authorizer/evidence requirement/rollback requirement, connecting directly to the Nexus governance work.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 1.Observe 2.Ask/Inquire 3.Retrieve Context 4.Establish Applicable Knowledge 5.Analyze 6.Decide 7.Authorize 8.Act 9.Observe Result 10.Produce Evidence 11.Verify 12.Update Knowledge — not every operation requires every stage explicitly, but the semantics must remain available.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the twelve-step operating lifecycle, elaborated per step: Observe produces an Observation, not a conclusion (examples: repository changed, infrastructure changed, proposal created, security finding, Nexus upgrade requested, production incident); Inquiry schema (subject,question,context,requester,purpose,scope); Retrieve Context resolves governed representations (current architecture, Softwareeinführungsprozess, IT Change Management, Nexus architecture, existing ADRs, infrastructure facts, previous decisions, applicable exceptions) rather than reconstructing from arbitrary documents; Establish Applicable Knowledge formalizes ApplicableKnowledge(t,scope,authority) — correct version/effective period/scope/authority/exceptions; Analyze produces an Analysis, not a Decision (worked Nexus-version-vs-target example with impact areas); Decide branches into AUTOMATIC/AUTHORIZED HUMAN/GOVERNANCE paths depending on risk/architecture-relevance/exception status, connecting to the Softwareeinführungsprozess/Change Management/Architecture Board discussion; Authorization remains separate from Decision (Approval ≠ ExecutionPermission, e.g. Board approves target architecture while Developer is authorized to implement it); Action carries ActionId/Actor/AuthorityContext/Target/Intent/Authorization/Timestamp/ExpectedEffect/EvidenceRequirements ('the operational form of the Action Kernel'); Observe Result records raw facts (not yet assurance conclusions); Evidence packages Observation+Source+Method+Timestamp+Context from sources like CI/CD, repository, runtime, infrastructure, test, static analysis, human review, agent analysis.

b_rows_sample.anchor: DecisionClass: TECHNICAL, OPERATIONAL, ARCHITECTURAL, GOVERNANCE, EXCEPTION — not every decision has the same authority requirement.
b_rows_sample.statement: Introduces a decision classification taxonomy, exact organizational mapping left to governance.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ExpectedArchitecture =? ObservedArchitecture, or Rule(x)=true? Result: PASS/FAIL/INCONCLUSIVE/NOT_APPLICABLE. No proof ≠ Proof of violation — INCONCLUSIVE must not silently become FAIL.
b_rows_sample.statement: Strongly retains the INCONCLUSIVE assurance verdict as epistemically distinct from FAIL, with an explicit statistical argument (P(violation|E) may be uncertain, but insufficient evidence must not be treated as proof of violation) — 'one of the strongest statistician-oriented safeguards in KnowledgeOS.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Raw Observation → Evidence → Analysis → Candidate Knowledge → Review → Governance → Authoritative Knowledge. L0 Raw Observation .. L5 Governed/Authoritative Knowledge.
b_rows_sample.statement: Restates the knowledge-promotion pipeline (Update Knowledge stage produces a KnowledgeCandidate, only the governance process elevates it to AuthoritativeKnowledge) and proposes a generic six-level epistemic-authority ladder L0-L5, names not necessarily final but the distinction architecturally valuable.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Confidence=0.98 but Authority=0. Confidence ≠ Authority. 500 agents repeating the same statement does not create authority — Authority(frequency) ≠ Authority(source).
b_rows_sample.statement: States two crucial invariants: confidence must never be confused with authority, and popularity/repetition must never be confused with truth/authority — 'precisely why provenance must be structural.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Source→Claim→Interpretation→Decision→Action→Observation→Evidence→Verification, plus Claim{derivedFrom,supportedBy,contextualizedBy,approvedBy,supersedes,contradictedBy}. CONTRADICTION_DETECTED as a first-class concept.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the operating knowledge-graph relationship model, and worked contradiction example (Rule R requires A, Observation shows A absent, another document says A is optional) — KnowledgeOS must not silently pick one but expose CONTRADICTION_DETECTED and route it through Contradiction->Inquiry->Evidence->Authority Resolution->Decision->Knowledge Update, 'exactly what a Knowledge Operating System should do.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Governance resolves which rule applies, which version is authoritative, who may decide, whether this is an exception, which interpretation is valid, when a new rule becomes effective — not merely 'approve documents.'
b_rows_sample.statement: Redefines Governance as a knowledge-resolution mechanism, more precise than 'document approval.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Domain Architect: knowledge and architecture boundary manager (interprets/models/questions/analyzes/proposes/reviews/governs/assures) depending on delegated authority, never silently becoming the source of organizational truth. Architecture Board: Architectural Authority evaluating Proposal/Context/Impact/Evidence/Risk/Principles/Existing Decisions to create GovernanceDecision. Developer: consumes governed context ('what architecture applies to this implementation?'). AI agent: a knowledge-mediated engineering actor (Governed Context+Reasoning+Authorized Capabilities+Evidence Production, not merely LLM+Tools). System actor: provides observational authority over its own state (Git: commit exists; CI: test executed; Runtime: container running; Nexus: repository exists) but not governance authority.
b_rows_sample.statement: Assigns operating roles per actor type, restating ObservationAuthority ≠ GovernanceAuthority for system actors.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Epistemic Authority (what is authoritative knowledge?), Governance Authority (what is approved?), Execution Authority (who may perform an action?), Observational Authority (what system can establish a fact?).
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a four-way authority decomposition proposed to become part of the KnowledgeOS constitutional model.

b_rows_sample.anchor: GOVERNANCE -authoritative knowledge-> KNOWLEDGE -context-> INQUIRY -analysis-> DECISION -authorization-> ACTION -execution-> OBSERVATION -evidence-> ASSURANCE -findings/proof-> GOVERNANCE.
b_rows_sample.statement: Presents the mature complete operating-loop diagram, and combines the previously separate Engineering and Governance Golden Traces into one 'KnowledgeOS Operating Golden Trace': Knowledge->Context->Inquiry->Decision->Authorization->Action->Observation->Evidence->Verification->Knowledge.

Gives a control-theory mathematical interpretation of the operating loop, a feedback-control system with organizational state S_t, action A_t, measurement method M_t, and applicable rule set R_t, described as a 'genuine feedback-control interpretation of KnowledgeOS.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Classical control: error→controller→automatic correction. KnowledgeOS: error→finding→decision→authorized correction. Assurance detects; Governance decides; Authorization permits; Engineering acts.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the crucial constraint distinguishing KnowledgeOS from an automatic controller — this four-part separation 'should become constitutional'; worked failure-handling example (Finding->Classification->Impact->Decision with outcomes FIX/ACCEPT RISK/APPROVE EXCEPTION/REJECT CHANGE/ROLLBACK/INVESTIGATE, the Assurance Engine not choosing among these without delegated authority) contrasting 'AI sees violation->AI changes code' (unsafe) with 'AI sees violation->Finding->Context->Decision authority->Authorized action' (KnowledgeOS's safer path), preventing 'AI governance by accident.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: No system observation, AI inference or engineering action automatically acquires governance authority merely by occurring.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes this single sentence as a constitutional statement protecting the architecture from a large class of future failures.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS remembers what was known, why it was believed, where it came from, who had authority, what decision was made, what action followed, what actually happened, what evidence was produced, whether it conformed, what was learned — substantially more powerful than a knowledge base. KnowledgeOS = Organizational Epistemic Infrastructure.
b_rows_sample.statement: Reframes KnowledgeOS as organizational memory and then as 'Organizational Epistemic Infrastructure' — concerned with how the organization establishes, preserves, contextualizes and validates what it treats as knowledge, explicitly framed as the destination the Chapter 4 validation pointed toward.

group_evidence.why_grouped: working_label token overlap Jaccard=0.50 (shared tokens: ['kos', 'model', 'operating'])

a_rows_sample.anchor: Given everything currently known, what should happen next? ... Lord(K_t,Z_t,G,C)\rightarrow a_t
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Lord's fundamental operator: Lord(K_t, Z_t=Zero(K_t,EC), G, C) -> a_t, the next action; framed as needing to answer 'given everything currently known, what should happen next?' without letting Lord become 'an uncontrolled LLM planner.'

type_signature.domain: KnowledgeState x ZeroResult x Goal x Constraints

a_rows_sample.anchor: Action=EpistemicAction\cup OperationalAction
a_rows_sample.statement: Separates two action categories: Epistemic action q: K_t -> K_{t+1} (e.g. query database, inspect configuration, search documentation, ask human, run test, verify firewall, compare documents) and Operational action a: W_t -> W_{t+1} (e.g. deploy, migrate, restart, modify configuration, create infrastructure); Action = EpistemicAction ∪ OperationalAction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Lord selects; Governance authorizes; Executor executes ... much safer than LLM\rightarrow Shell
a_rows_sample.statement: Lord proposes a CandidateAction; a governed execution layer separately checks Authorized?/Safe?/ContractSatisfied?/Allowed?; therefore 'Lord selects; Governance authorizes; Executor executes,' explicitly contrasted as much safer than a direct LLM -> Shell architecture.

a_rows_sample.anchor: \mathcal A(K_t) ... Lord cannot choose an action outside \mathcal A
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a bounded candidate action space A(K_t) (e.g. {QueryFirewall, InspectBackup, AskArchitect, RunRestoreTest, MigrateNexus, DoNothing}); Lord cannot choose an action outside this set.

a_rows_sample.anchor: a^*=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal A} VOI(a) ... insufficient
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects a naive first formulation a*=argmax_a VOI(a) as insufficient because VOI captures only information/decision value and ignores authorization, safety, cost, urgency, dependencies, and reversibility.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A=(Purpose,ExpectedGain,Cost,Risk,Urgency,Reversibility,Authorization,Dependencies,Deadline) ... resist prematurely creating Score(A)=0.83
a_rows_sample.statement: Represents an action as a nine-dimensional vector A=(Purpose, ExpectedGain, Cost, Risk, Urgency, Reversibility, Authorization, Dependencies, Deadline), explicitly warning against prematurely collapsing it to a scalar Score(A)=0.83 which 'would hide semantics.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Feasible(a,K_t,C) ... RunRestoreTest ... Feasible=True ... MigrateNexus RollbackVerified=unknown ... Feasible=False
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Feasible(a,K_t,C), worked with two examples: RunRestoreTest is Feasible=True (all preconditions available/acceptable), while MigrateNexus is Feasible=False when RollbackVerified=unknown is a blocking condition.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A_{feasible}=\{a\in A\mid Feasible(a,K,C)\} ... a^*=Select(A_{feasible},Objective)
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes the two-stage algorithm: first compute A_feasible = {a in A | Feasible(a,K,C)}, then a* = Select(A_feasible, Objective); Lord's two responsibilities are therefore (1) remove impossible/unauthorized actions, (2) choose among the remaining — 'Feasibility -> Optimization.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Zero={RollbackUnknown, FirewallConflicted, ApprovalMissing} ... ApprovalMissing is a hard governance blocker ... MigrateNexus is infeasible
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: given three concurrent Zero gaps and four candidate actions (run restore test, query firewall, ask Architecture Board, execute migration), a hard governance blocker (ApprovalMissing) renders MigrateNexus infeasible, so Lord must choose among the information/governance actions instead.

a_rows_sample.anchor: RootGap(Z)=r_1 ... Lord should not necessarily target r_3. It should target the root gap
a_rows_sample.statement: Root-gap analysis reusing the dependency chain r1=BackupExists -> r2=RestoreValidated -> r3=RollbackVerified: if r3=Unknown is caused by r1=Unknown, Lord should target RootGap(Z)=r1, not r3 — described as 'graph reasoning, not LLM intuition,' making Lord 'more efficient.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: BackupExists -> RestoreEnvironmentAvailable -> RestoreTest -> RollbackVerified -> MigrationEligible
a_rows_sample.statement: Depicts the action dependency graph Lord can traverse to reach the root-gap-resolving action.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_{t+1}=Update(K_t,E_q) ... VOI(q) ... depends on a model ... ExpectedOutcomeModel(q)
a_rows_sample.statement: For an epistemic action q, defines K_{t+1}=Update(K_t,E_q) and states VOI(q) requires access to an ExpectedOutcomeModel(q), reiterating that VOI depends on a model (as established in the prior evidence/VOI thread).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Outcome(q)=\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\} with probabilities or qualitative likelihoods where appropriate
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes expected from guaranteed outcomes: querying a database has an expected result (record found) but may fail; Outcome(q) is a set of possible outcomes with probabilities or qualitative likelihoods, letting Lord evaluate expected consequences.

a_rows_sample.anchor: EU(q)=\sum_e P(e\mid q,K)\max_a EU(a\mid K,e) ... VOI(q)=EU(q)-EU(a^*) ... optional specialized engine, not part of the epistemic kernel
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives the classical statistical/decision-theoretic version: EU(q)=sum_e P(e|q,K) max_a EU(a|K,e); VOI(q)=EU(q)-EU(a*); explicitly classified as 'an optional specialized engine, not part of the epistemic kernel.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: HighValue>MediumValue>LowValue ... q_1\succeq q_2 ... KnowledgeOS should not manufacture probabilities
a_rows_sample.statement: Where probabilities are unavailable, proposes a qualitative ordering (HighValue > MediumValue > LowValue) or a partial preference relation q1 ⪰ q2, motivated by the principle that 'KnowledgeOS should not manufacture probabilities.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: q_1: resolve governance blocker ... q_2: collect additional architecture detail ... q_1\succ q_2 ... No numerical score is needed
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked example showing a qualitative preference (q1 directly unblocks the goal, q2 does not, so q1 ≻ q2) can be established without any numerical score — 'preferable when quantitative utility is unavailable.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Prefer(a_1,a_2\mid K,G,C) ... rather than assuming Score(a) ... a_1\succ a_2, a_2\succ a_1, or a_1\sim a_2
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes Lord's decision relation Prefer(a1,a2|K,G,C) with outcomes {a1≻a2, a2≻a1, a1~a2} rather than assuming a scalar Score(a); a1~a2 means 'both are equally defensible under current knowledge.'

type_signature.domain: Action x Action x KnowledgeState x Goal x Constraints

a_rows_sample.anchor: IndeterminatePreference\rightarrow HumanDecision ... rather than arbitrary AI selection
a_rows_sample.statement: When a1~a2 and the system cannot distinguish them by governed criteria, Lord may ask for human preference: IndeterminatePreference -> HumanDecision, rather than arbitrary AI selection.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Safety(a,K,C) must hold ... RollbackVerified=Unknown ... Safety=False ... MigrateNexus\notin A_{feasible}
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Safety(a,K,C) as a required precondition before selecting an operational action; e.g. ProductionMigration requiring RollbackVerified=True fails Safety when RollbackVerified=Unknown, excluding MigrateNexus from A_feasible.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Authorized(a,C) must be true ... rm -rf ... Authorized=False ... Capability\neq Authority
a_rows_sample.statement: An AI may be technically capable of an action (e.g. 'rm -rf ...') yet Authorized(a,C)=False makes it non-candidate: 'Capability ≠ Authority' — 'a fundamental separation.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Lord = selects the next useful action ... Sarathi = determines what decision should be made
b_rows_sample.statement: Opens by distinguishing Lord ('selects the next useful action,' e.g. 'perform a restore test') from Sarathi ('determines what decision should be made,' e.g. migrate/postpone/change plan/stop given resulting knowledge).

b_rows_sample.anchor: D=\{Migrate,Postpone,ChangePlan,Reject\} ... Decision\neq Action
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the decision set D (e.g. {Migrate, Postpone, ChangePlan, Reject}) as distinct from the executable action set A (e.g. a single decision d=Migrate may require several actions {Backup, RestoreTest, FirewallValidation, Approval, Migration}) — Decision ≠ Action.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Lord: (K,Z,G,C)\rightarrow A ... Sarathi: (K,G,D,C,P)\rightarrow d
b_rows_sample.statement: States the precise operator distinction: Lord: (K,Z,G,C)->A (chooses what to do next to advance the process); Sarathi: (K,G,D,C,P)->d (chooses which decision is justified given current knowledge and decision model P).

type_signature.domain: KnowledgeState x Goal x DecisionSet x Constraints x Policy

b_rows_sample.anchor: Consequences(d_1) ... OutcomeModel(d,K)
b_rows_sample.statement: Decision reasoning requires knowing Consequences(d) (e.g. for d1=Migrate: Success, Failure, DataLoss, Downtime, Rollback), formalized as requiring an OutcomeModel(d,K).

b_rows_sample.anchor: U(Success)=+100, U(Failure)=-50, U(DataLoss)=-1000 ... illustrative only ... must never be invented by the AI and presented as organizational truth
b_rows_sample.statement: Introduces a utility function U(o) over outcomes with illustrative example values, explicitly warning these numbers 'must never be invented by the AI and presented as organizational truth.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: EU(d\mid K)=\sum_o P(o\mid d,K)U(o) ... d^*=\arg\max_d EU(d\mid K) subject to governance and safety constraints
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines expected utility EU(d|K)=sum_o P(o|d,K)U(o) and d*=argmax_d EU(d|K), explicitly subject to governance and safety constraints — 'a mathematically well-defined decision mechanism.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: P(o\mid d,K) cannot reasonably be established. We must not invent it ... Preference(d_1,d_2) or Dominates(d_1,d_2)
b_rows_sample.statement: When probability cannot reasonably be established, prohibits inventing it and instead allows qualitative Preference(d1,d2) or Dominates(d1,d2) (e.g. 'if migration is unauthorized, postponement dominates migration' — no probability necessary).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Feasible(d,K,C) ... Migrate requires RollbackVerified=True ... Feasible(Migrate)=False ... should not matter how attractive migration appears economically
b_rows_sample.statement: Before utility calculation, Sarathi must determine Feasible(d,K,C); e.g. Migrate requiring RollbackVerified=True is Feasible=False when RollbackVerified=Unknown, regardless of economic attractiveness.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Hard constraint C(d)=True ... Preference d_1\succ d_2 ... Constraints filter; Utility/preferences select
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes hard constraints (must hold, e.g. ProductionChangeAuthorized) from preferences among permissible decisions (e.g. prefer lower expected downtime): 'Constraints filter; Utility/preferences select.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: EU(Migrate)=95 ... EU(Postpone)=60 ... Authorized(Migrate)=False ... Migrate is eliminated before utility optimization ... Utility cannot override governance
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example showing higher expected utility (Migrate=95 vs Postpone=60) does not matter once Authorized(Migrate)=False eliminates it before optimization — 'Utility cannot override governance.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: DecisionModel=(Outcomes,Constraints,Preferences,Utilities,Uncertainty,Policy) ... Sarathi(K,D,DecisionModel)\rightarrow DecisionResult
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a six-component DecisionModel=(Outcomes, Constraints, Preferences, Utilities, Uncertainty, Policy) and Sarathi(K,D,DecisionModel)->DecisionResult.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Decision: POSTPONE ... Reason: rollback capability not established ... Blocking requirements: RollbackVerified ... Evidence basis: E17,E22,E31 ... Now the decision is auditable
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked full auditable DecisionResult record for a POSTPONE decision containing reason, blocking requirements, alternative feasibility, evidence basis, decision model version, and authorization status — contrasted with returning a bare 'MIGRATE' label.

b_rows_sample.anchor: DecisionProvenance(d) ... K_t+Contract+Policy+Model+Evidence\rightarrow d ... Decision must be reproducible
b_rows_sample.statement: Requires DecisionProvenance(d) tracing K_t+Contract+Policy+Model+Evidence -> d, so 'Decision must be reproducible.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Decision_t remains associated with K_t ... Decision_{t+1} is calculated from K_{t+1} ... Decision is time-indexed
b_rows_sample.statement: A historical decision (e.g. today's Postpone) must not be rewritten when tomorrow's new evidence would produce Migrate; Decision_t stays tied to K_t, and Decision_{t+1} is separately computed from K_{t+1} — 'Decision is time-indexed.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Stability(d,K) as sensitivity to plausible changes in the knowledge state
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines decision Stability(d,K) conceptually as sensitivity to plausible changes in the knowledge state, motivated by the concern that small evidence changes flipping Migrate<->Postpone indicate an unstable decision.

b_rows_sample.anchor: P(Success)=0.91 ... threshold 0.90 ... Migrate ... if a small uncertainty could make P(Success)=0.88 ... DecisionFragility=High
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: a decision that barely clears its threshold (P(Success)=0.91 vs threshold 0.90) but could plausibly drop to 0.88 under small uncertainty should be reported as DecisionFragility=High rather than simply 'Migrate.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: P(Success)\ge\theta ... \theta must come from governance/domain policy. The AI cannot invent it
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes threshold decisions P(Success)>=theta (e.g. theta=0.95: P=0.97=>Migrate, P=0.72=>Postpone), explicitly requiring theta to come from governance/domain policy — 'the AI cannot invent it.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Probability=Unknown ... We should not substitute P=0.5 ... Unknown+CriticalRisk\rightarrow Postpone
